name: Tomas Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I milk a hundred and eighty Holsteins at Brookside, which is a dairy farm I rent on a long lease from a church trust. Since 2019 the cows have milked themselves, more or less, through two milking robots. They walk in when they want, a laser finds the teats, and the machine logs everything. So my day starts at six on the laptop in the kitchen, looking at which cows are down on milk or haven't visited, and then I go out and find them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the puzzle. Cow 412 drops three litres and walks a bit slow, and you work out whether it's her feet, her udder or her mood. What wears me out is the alarms. The robot texts me at three in the morning when a cup falls off, and my wife Ilse says she married a farmer, not a fire station.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pavel, my herdsman, has been with me twelve years. He came from abroad with almost nothing and now he knows the cows better than me. And our vet, Dr Achebe, comes every two weeks. Ilse does the calves and the books.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I ask one to read the robot data and tell me which cows to worry about, and I use it to draft letters to the milk buyer and the trust. I was the first in our discussion group to get robots, and they all laughed. Now four of them have them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a shame, honestly, because it could do more. At the discussion group I'd be the one saying, look, the robots already changed dairying, so don't tell me AI is just a search engine. But I'd also say, fine, it's still useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's no change. I'm already using it every day for the herd data. The milk price is set by the processor, and that's still the thing that decides whether I have a good year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd probably pay for a better herd-health program, about nine hundred a year, that spots lameness from how the cows walk past a camera. I'd keep pushing the others in the group to try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly disappointed, maybe, like a film that never gets going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the milk price decides your year. What's it doing to you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's swinging. Last spring it dropped six pence a litre in two months, and on our volume that's about fifteen thousand off the year. No robot fixes that. The processor holds all the cards, and that's the thing I'd change if I could change one thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the discussion group still laughs at you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Henrik Bauer. He milks sixty cows in a parlour his father built, and he says the cows like his singing. Maybe they do. He's also seventy-one and his back is gone, and nobody's coming to take over.

S0.say: I'd say it's a shame AI isn't doing more, because robots already changed dairying. But it's still a useful tool, and I'd keep pushing the others to try it.
S0.think: Privately it changes nothing for me, because I already use it daily for herd data. The processor's milk price still decides whether I have a good year.
S0.do: Pays about nine hundred a year for a herd-health program that spots lameness from camera footage. Keeps encouraging the discussion group to try new tools.
S0.feel: Calm, slightly disappointed that the change never gets going.
S0.quote: He milks sixty cows in a parlour his father built, and he says the cows like his singing.
S0.fieldNote: He is impatient for more, not less, technology. His real complaint is the power of the milk processor, which is a progressive grievance from a man who loves gadgets. Henrik is the counter-example he keeps returning to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is good for most people, it gives time to adjust. But I'd also say companies not hiring beginners is a disaster for farming, where we already can't find young people. I'd push for apprenticeships paid for by the companies making the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, slow is fine, I'm already ahead. The worry is succession. Neither of my daughters wants the farm, and if young people can't get a start anywhere, maybe one of them comes home. Or maybe nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on an apprentice from the college, which I've been saying I'd do for three years. That's about fourteen thousand a year in wages after the grant. I'd teach them the robots and the cows together, because that's what dairying will be. And I'd ask Pavel to mentor them, with a pay rise for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit of worry about who comes after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe a daughter comes home. Would you want that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part of me would love it. Anna is a software tester in the city, and she'd actually be brilliant with the robots. But I wouldn't want her here because she had nowhere else to go. I want her here because she chose it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourteen thousand for an apprentice is real money. Can you carry it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just. We've got about four months of costs in the bank. It means no new tractor for another two years, and I'd be running the old one with the dodgy hydraulics. But a tractor won't run the farm when I'm seventy.

S1.say: I'd say slow change gives people time, but companies not hiring beginners is a disaster for farming. Companies making the money should pay for apprenticeships.
S1.think: Privately I'm already ahead, so slow is fine. My worry is succession, since neither daughter wants the farm and I don't know who comes after me.
S1.do: Takes on a college apprentice at about fourteen thousand a year after the grant and trains them on robots and cows together. Gives Pavel a pay rise to mentor them and delays a new tractor two years.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with some worry about who comes after him.
S1.quote: But a tractor won't run the farm when I'm seventy.
S1.fieldNote: He turns a hiring slowdown into a succession question. His wish for his daughter to come home is honest and careful: by choice, not by necessity. He spends from a modest cushion on a person instead of a machine, which is notable for someone who loves machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should share the gains, a shorter working week, help for retraining, maybe a basic income. I'd say it at the discussion group and online, and I'd get into arguments with Henrik, who'd say it's all handouts. I'd also say the new AI jobs should be in the countryside too, not just the cities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm all right, cows don't care about office work. But Anna is a software tester, and testing is just the kind of routine work these assistants would take. And Ilse's brother runs a small accounting firm in town, and that's a whole business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Anna over a video call and talk about her options, because she'd tell me before she'd tell her mum. I'd say if she wants to, she can come home and run the robot side, the data, properly, and I'd pay her. And I'd use the AI more myself to cut our accountant's bill, which is a bit grim given it's Ilse's brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, but for Anna, and for the whole idea that a degree keeps you safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd cut the accountant's bill, and the accountant is your brother-in-law. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Yes. That's the problem with this stuff, isn't it? You say you want to protect jobs, and then you save four hundred pounds by doing it yourself with a chatbot. I'd probably still pay him, if I'm honest, for Christmas dinner's sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the job on the farm look like for Anna?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching the herd data, setting up the cameras, talking to the robot company when it breaks, which is a lot. It's a real job, maybe three days a week. She'd also have to help with calving, and she used to faint at the sight of blood, so we'd see.

S2.say: I'd say the government should share the gains with a shorter week, retraining and maybe a basic income. And the new AI jobs should come to the countryside, not just the cities.
S2.think: Privately I'm fine, cows don't care about office work. But my daughter Anna is a software tester and my brother-in-law runs an accounting firm, and both are exactly the routine work at risk.
S2.do: Has a video call with Anna about her options and offers her a paid three-day-a-week job running the farm's robot data. Considers doing his own books with AI, though he'd probably keep paying his brother-in-law.
S2.feel: Uneasy for Anna and for the idea that a degree keeps you safe.
S2.quote: You say you want to protect jobs, and then you save four hundred pounds by doing it yourself with a chatbot.
S2.fieldNote: He catches his own contradiction about the accountant before I could, and laughs at it. His instinct is to pull Anna into the farm and give her the technical side. Progressive views and early adoption sit side by side without much friction, until it's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a real share of the gains. If shares and houses boom, tax them, properly, and use it to look after people. I'd go to the protests. I'd say it louder than I've ever said anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The honest bit is that my lease is with a church trust, and if land prices boom, they might want to sell or put the rent up. A lot of the trust's money is in shares, so they'll feel rich, but trusts get greedy too. On the cow side, nothing changes, the milk still needs drinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the trust in the first month and ask to fix the rent for ten years, in exchange for me putting in solar panels on the shed roof. I'd talk to the milk buyer about a longer contract. And I'd get Anna home properly if she lost her job, full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The lease is the thing I can't control, and it's everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Anna loses her job and comes home full time, what does that do to the farm's money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's tight. Another wage, and the farm makes about forty-five thousand in a good year after everything. She'd have to take less than she earned in the city, and we'd have to make the farm earn more. Maybe she'd find ways I haven't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said trusts get greedy too. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen them. A church trust down the valley sold a farm to a pension fund three years ago, after the tenant had been there forty years. They said it was their duty to the money. That's what scares me.

S3.say: I'd say tax the share and house boom properly and use it to look after people. I'd go to the protests and say it louder than ever.
S3.think: Privately the lease worries me most, because a church trust with booming land could sell or raise the rent. The cows themselves won't notice anything.
S3.do: Asks the trust in the first month to fix the rent for ten years in exchange for solar panels on the shed roof. Seeks a longer milk contract and brings Anna home full time if she loses her job.
S3.feel: Anxious, because the lease is out of his control and it's everything.
S3.quote: A church trust down the valley sold a farm to a pension fund three years ago, after the tenant had been there forty years.
S3.fieldNote: As a tenant, the threat to him is land values, not machines, and he sees it immediately. His offer of solar panels for a fixed rent shows his habit of trading technology for security. The story of the neighbouring trust is clearly something he's carried for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms are coming anyway, and the question is who owns them. If it's only the big companies, small farms die. I'd push for co-ops, public loans, so ordinary farmers can buy in. I'd say it at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm actually ready for this one. I put robots in my milking parlour seven years ago. The cows adjusted in a fortnight. The farmers around here still haven't. My worry is Pavel. If robots can feed calves and scrape yards and catch lame cows, what's Pavel for?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at a feeding robot and a yard scraper, about sixty thousand together, probably on a lease. But first I'd sit Pavel down and make him the robot man, the one who fixes and runs them, with training from the company paid by me. I'd also talk to Dr Achebe, because if cameras spot illness earlier, she might come less, and her practice is already struggling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited too, which feels wrong to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does it feel wrong to say you're excited?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know what it means for people. I'm excited about a machine that might put Henrik out of business and make Pavel's job smaller. But I'd be lying if I said I wasn't curious to see a robot calve a heifer. Both things are true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Pavel, the day you sit him down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Pavel, I'm buying machines, and I'm not buying them to replace you. I need someone who understands the cows and the machines, and that's you. Then I'd put the training course in his hand so he knew I meant it. He's been let down by bosses before.

S4.say: I'd say farm robots are coming anyway and the real question is who owns them. I'd push for co-ops and public loans so ordinary farmers can buy in.
S4.think: Privately I'm ready, because I put robots in my milking parlour years ago. My worry is Pavel, my herdsman, and what's left for him if robots feed calves and catch lame cows.
S4.do: Leases a feeding robot and yard scraper worth about sixty thousand. Pays for Pavel's training to become the farm's robot technician and talks with the vet about how earlier detection might affect her practice.
S4.feel: Anxious, but excited too, and uncomfortable about the excitement.
S4.quote: I put robots in my milking parlour seven years ago. The cows adjusted in a fortnight. The farmers around here still haven't.
S4.fieldNote: He's the only farmer here who sees the robot picture as partly good news. His excitement makes him uneasy, because he knows who loses. He plans to protect Pavel by retraining him, and he names the vet as a second casualty nobody else mentions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fourth one, the fast one, because of the lease. Robots I can handle, it's the land that frightens me. What would help is security for tenant farmers, rent fixed by law for good tenants, and public loans for co-ops so small farms can own the machines together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. The robots are good for them, honestly. They milk when they like, they're calmer. People think it's cruel. It isn't. The cruel thing is a man with a bad back milking sixty cows at five in the morning because nobody's coming to help.

headlineQuote: I put robots in my milking parlour seven years ago. The cows adjusted in a fortnight. The farmers around here still haven't.
portrait: Tomas Ziegler is fifty-eight and milks a hundred and eighty cows with two robots on a farm he rents from a church trust. He's an early adopter with progressive views, impatient for change but worried about who owns the machines and who gets left behind. Through the office-job scenarios his worry is his daughter Anna, a software tester, whom he'd bring home to run the farm's data. The fast scenario frightens him more than the robot one, because rising land prices could cost him his lease, while robots he feels ready for, as long as his herdsman Pavel comes along.
biggestWorry: The fast scenario worries him most, because a land boom could lead the church trust to sell his farm or raise the rent.
whatWouldHelp: Legal rent security for good tenant farmers, and public loans for co-ops so small farms can own robots together.
